decks.name: LeetCode #1851 - Minimum Interval to Include Each Query
decks.description: Find the smallest interval that contains each query point

cards.question: Minimum Interval to Include Each Query: You are given a 2D integer array intervals, where intervals[i] = [left_i, right_i] describes the ith interval starting at left_i and ending at right_i (inclusive). The size of an interval is defined as the number of integers it contains, or more formally right_i - left_i + 1. You are also given an integer array queries. The answer to the jth query is the size of the smallest interval i such that left_i <= queries[j] <= right_i. If no such interval exists, the answer is -1. Return an array containing the answers to the queries.

solutions.name: Brute Force
solutions.explanation: For each query, check every interval to find the smallest one containing it. Iterate through all intervals and check if query point falls within bounds (left <= query <= right). Track minimum interval size found. If interval contains query and is smaller than current minimum, update minimum. If no interval contains query, return -1. Simple but inefficient as we check all intervals for every query. O(m*n) time checking every query-interval pair.

solutions.name: Sweep Line Algorithm
solutions.explanation: Create events for interval starts, ends, and queries, then process chronologically. Build event list with interval start (type 0), query (type 1), and interval end (type 2). Sort events by time, with type as tie-breaker (ends before queries). Use min heap to track active interval sizes and inactive array to mark ended intervals. When processing interval start, add size to heap. When processing interval end, mark interval as inactive. When processing query, remove inactive intervals from heap top and get minimum size from heap. This processes intervals and queries in chronological order efficiently. O((n+m)log(n+m)) time from sorting and heap operations.

solutions.name: Min Heap
solutions.explanation: Sort intervals by start time, process queries in sorted order using min heap. First sort intervals by start time. Process queries in sorted order (using dictionary to restore original order). For each query, add all intervals starting at or before query to min heap (storing size and end time). Remove intervals from heap that end before query. Top of heap gives minimum size interval containing query. This ensures we only add each interval once and remove intervals efficiently. Much better than brute force. O(nlogn + mlogm) time from sorting intervals and queries, heap operations are bounded.

solutions.name: Min Segment Tree (Lazy Propagation)
solutions.explanation: Use coordinate compression with segment tree and lazy propagation for range updates. First compress coordinates by collecting all unique points from intervals and queries, creating mapping from value to index. Build segment tree over compressed coordinate space. For each interval, perform range update on compressed range with interval size using lazy propagation (deferred updates). For each query, perform point query on compressed coordinate to get minimum interval size. Lazy propagation allows efficient range updates by deferring updates to children until needed. Propagation pushes lazy values down tree. Good for many overlapping intervals. O((n+m)logk) time where k is unique points.

solutions.timeDescription: Collecting unique points is O(n+m), sorting unique points is O(klogk) where k is unique points, building segment tree is O(k), each interval update is O(logk) for n intervals, each query is O(logk) for m queries, total O((n+m)logk)
solutions.spaceDescription: Segment tree stores O(4k) nodes, lazy propagation array stores O(4k) values, compression map stores O(k) mappings, points array stores O(n+m) values before deduplication, answer array stores O(m) results
solutions.exampleWalkthrough: Given intervals=[[1,4],[2,4]], queries=[2,3]: Collect points: [1,4,2,4,2,3]. Unique sorted: [1,2,3,4]. Compress: {1:0, 2:1, 3:2, 4:3}. Build segment tree over indices 0-3. Update range [0,3] with size 4 for interval [1,4]. Update range [1,3] with size 3 for interval [2,4]. Tree now has: idx 0 has min 4, idx 1-3 have min 3. Query at 2 (compressed idx 1): returns 3. Query at 3 (compressed idx 2): returns 3. Return [3,3].
